reading.translation:
Socrates discusses education with Aristippus. He sets two young men before him in the discussion: one will rule, while the other does not wish to rule. What education suits the young men?

The young man who will rule does not always seek his own pleasure. For there are tasks which do not wait. The friend whom it is necessary to help is in danger.

Socrates asks about food, drink, and sleep. The ruler, whom the friends were calling, was already working. He is not always sitting in the house.

Work is often outdoors. The men feel the cold and the summer heat. The road has a deep ravine; the toil is heavy.

Aristippus says, “I do not wish to rule. Office brings many tasks. I seek a life which has pleasure.” Socrates examines the claim.

Who chooses the education? Whom do the tasks help? Does the person ruling others master himself? We now investigate these matters. For a fine argument does not resolve every difficulty.

blocks.title: παιδεία: education with a purpose
body: παιδεία concerns formation and education, not only classroom instruction. Its family includes παῖς, “child,” and παιδεύω, “educate.” A shared root helps recognition but does not make every word mean the same thing.
Ask what kind of person the education aims to form. In the reading, the answer depends on the proposed way of life. The related nouns name a process and a person; the verb names the action.

sections.title: 1. Relative pronouns: agreement and case
body: A relative pronoun links a description to an antecedent. It agrees with that antecedent in gender and number, but its case comes from its role inside the relative clause. In βίον ... ὃς ἡδονὴν ἔχει, βίον is accusative while ὃς is nominative because it is the subject of ἔχει.

First bracket the relative clause, then ask who does what within it. Do not simply copy the antecedent’s case. The relative has a rough breathing and usually an accent: distinguish ὅς from the article ὁ.

sections.title: 2. Neuter nouns with an -εσ- stem
body: In nouns such as τὸ γένος, the sigma between vowels disappears and the neighboring vowels contract: γένεσ-ος becomes γένους. The nominative and accusative singular end in -ος; this does not make the noun masculine or second declension.

The article reveals gender and case. Learn nominative plus genitive together. Plural γένη is nominative or accusative, while γενῶν is genitive plural. The same pattern explains ψύχους and θέρους in the reading.

sections.title: 3. Adjectives in -ύς, -εῖα, -ύ
body: These adjectives have a masculine and neuter pattern different from their feminine pattern: βαθύς, βαθεῖα, βαθύ. The feminine declines like a first-declension adjective, while masculine and neuter use stems in -υ/-ε.

An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number, and case. A ravine is feminine: βαθεῖαν χαράδραν. A burden can be described by neuter βαρύ. Accent and breathing belong to the written form; learn whole forms rather than stripping them away.

sections.title: 4. Putting clauses and noun forms together
body: A relative clause can interrupt the main statement. Find the main subject and verb first, then insert the description. In ὁ ἄρχων, ὃν οἱ φίλοι ἐκάλουν, ἐπόνει, the ruler was working; the friends were calling him.

Use noun endings to find the dependents of a verb or preposition. τοῦ ψύχους is a genitive noun, not a comparative adjective. Forms that look unusual become manageable when you identify article, stem, and clause role in that order.

sections.title: Meet the Memorabilia: an argument with Aristippus
body: In Memorabilia 2.1, Xenophon’s Socrates questions Aristippus about the education of someone intended to rule. Food, drink, sleep, heat, and cold become tests of whether a person can put a responsibility before an immediate comfort.

Aristippus supplies resistance: he does not simply ask how to become the ruler Socrates imagines. Read his preference for another kind of life as part of the argument. Xenophon presents a crafted exchange, not a neutral survey of all Athenian educational practices.

sections.title: Education beyond a classroom
body: The passage places education in the body’s routines as well as in speech. A ruler may have to work when tired or face a difficult environment. These examples make an abstract question—what kind of life should one prepare for?—concrete.

Our ravine and work scene are teaching arrangements. They let relatives identify the person who will rule, the friend who needs help, and the life someone chooses. Do not turn every descriptive sentence into a new historical fact about Aristippus.

sections.title: Who chooses the training?
body: A training program has a purpose, a designer, and a person who bears its costs. Socrates starts with the prospective ruler’s obligations; Aristippus challenges the desirability of that role. These are different starting points, not just different levels of effort.

Imagine designing training for a guide responsible for companions on a journey. Explain why each exercise is relevant. Then ask which hardship would add no useful skill. Discipline needs a reason, not merely a reputation for toughness.

sections.title: Follow the relative, follow the responsibility
body: Write three English clauses: “the person who leads,” “the friend whom we help,” and “the work that cannot wait.” Decide who is the subject within each clause.

Then locate ὃς, ᾧ, and ἃ in the reading. The case changes because the role changes. Grammar makes the network of responsibilities visible: the leader is not the subject of every action, and the person helped is not necessarily the one giving orders.
